e.meaning: most holy (as a form of Ariana)
e.etymology: A spelling of Ariana, which descends from the Greek name Ariadne, most holy. For Afghan and Iranian families it also recalls Aryana, an old name for the lands of the Iranian plateau.
e.note: The spelling contains Aryan, a word many Americans associate with Nazi racial ideology.

e.etymology: The Arabic and Swahili name of Eve, from Arabic Hawwa, matching Hebrew Chavah, living one. It is widely used by Muslim families across Africa.

e.meaning: gracious, dear (as a form of Milena)
e.etymology: A spelling of Milena, a Slavic name from the element mil, gracious or dear, written to show the long E. The same spelling belongs to a fighter in the Mortal Kombat video games.

assoc.t: Mileena, masked assassin of the Mortal Kombat games

e.etymology: A 20th-century coinage from Sheryl or Sheri with Lyn. In the United States it is used mostly by Spanish-speaking families, who know it from the Mexican actress Sherlyn.
From an English and Scottish surname, son of Gibb, a medieval short form of Gilbert. Its use as a first name is recent.

assoc.t: Gibson guitars, maker of the Les Paul
gibson, a martini garnished with a pickled onion

e.etymology: A respelling of Sienna, from the color sienna, an earthy reddish-brown pigment named for the Tuscan city of Siena.
From Arabic rashad, right guidance or good sense, the verbal noun of rashida, to follow the right path. It has been common among Black American families since the mid-1970s.
namesakes: Rashad Evans (former UFC light heavyweight champion)

assoc.t: Phylicia Rashad, The Cosby Show actress (surname)

e.etymology: A pet form of Emma and Emilia that is a full name in Finland and Germany. Emma is from a Germanic element meaning whole or universal. In the United States it also serves as a spelling of Emmy.

assoc.t: the Emmy Awards, television's top honors (same sound)

e.etymology: Coined about 1540 by the Earl of Surrey as a poetic name for Lady Elizabeth Fitzgerald, one of the Fitzgeralds. It became the feminine of Gerald, a Germanic name from spear and rule, in the 19th century.
namesakes: Geraldine Ferraro (first woman on a major-party presidential ticket)
Geraldine Chaplin (actress, daughter of Charlie Chaplin)

e.etymology: An American coinage in use since the 1970s, probably based on the Irish names Brennan or Brendan. Its meaning is not settled.
The French form of Anthony, from the Roman family name Antonius, whose source is unknown and possibly Etruscan. American use rose in the 1970s and produced spellings such as Antwan and Antwon.
namesakes: Antoine de Saint-Exupery (author of The Little Prince)

e.etymology: A modern American name, usually a blend of the Ka- prefix with Miya or Amiya; Kamiyah is the more common spelling. Kamiya is also a Japanese surname.
Borrowed from Hindi Vivan, traced to a Sanskrit word for plaiting or twisting. Indian baby-name books usually gloss it as full of life, and it rose sharply in the 2010s.
A spelling of Mariah, an English form of Maria and Mary, from Hebrew Miryam. It also matches Mariyah, the Arabic form borne by Maria the Copt, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad.

From Greek Linos, of uncertain meaning, often linked to linon, flax. In myth Linus was a musician, son of Apollo and teacher of Orpheus; a Linus greets Timothy in the New Testament and is counted the second pope.
namesakes: Linus van Pelt (Peanuts character with the security blanket)

assoc.t: Linus, the Peanuts boy with the security blanket

e.etymology: The Hawaiian form of John, borrowed from English and fitted to Hawaiian sounds. John goes back to Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
A respelling of Riley, an English surname meaning rye clearing and also a form of the Irish surname Reilly. The Rh- opening follows Rhys and Rhett.
A pet form of Raizel, from Yiddish royz, rose. It is used mainly in Hasidic and other Orthodox Jewish communities, where pet forms are often registered as full names.
A spelling of Inaya, from Arabic inayah, care or solicitude, often understood as God's care. The doubled a shows the long vowel and is common among South Asian Muslim families.
A Latin American spelling of Juliet, popular in Colombia. Juliet is from Italian Giulietta, a diminutive of Giulia, from the Roman family name Julius.

assoc.t: Juliet of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet (same sound)

e.etymology: From a Norman baronial surname taken from places in France named for a Gallo-Roman owner called Thracius, the Thracian. As a girls' name, popular in the 1960s and 1970s, it was also taken as a pet form of Theresa.
From an English and Scottish surname that began as a nickname, from Middle English tod, fox. It was a popular American first name in the 1960s and 1970s.
namesakes: Todd Phillips (director of The Hangover and Joker)

assoc.t: Sweeney Todd, the demon barber of Fleet Street (surname)

e.etymology: A spelling of Arianna, the Italian form of the Greek name Ariadne, from Cretan Greek ari, most, and adnos, holy. In myth Ariadne helped Theseus find his way out of the Labyrinth.
e.note: The spelling contains Aryan, a word many Americans associate with Nazi racial ideology.

e.etymology: A modern American coinage with no documented source. It echoes Malaysia and Asia, both used as girls' names, and the many names that open with Ala-.
A name used by Mexican American families since the 1990s, also spelled Yareli. Its source is not documented.
The Ashkenazi and Yiddish pronunciation of Hebrew Yehudit, the name English renders as Judith. It is the feminine of Yehudah, Judah, and belongs to the heroine of the Book of Judith.
A modern American coinage that adds the -lyn ending to Blake, an English surname from Old English words for dark or for pale.
From the English word charity in its biblical sense of Christian love, Latin caritas, as in faith, hope and charity (1 Corinthians 13). The Puritans were the first to use it as a name.

assoc.t: charity, giving to those in need

e.etymology: The Russian and Georgian form of the biblical Tamar, Hebrew for date palm. Queen Tamar ruled Georgia's medieval golden age, and English speakers adopted Tamara in the 20th century.
namesakes: Tamara Tunie (Law and Order: SVU actress)

e.meaning: fallow land; or follower of Saint Faolan
e.etymology: A spelling of Leland, a surname traced either to McClelland, Irish Mac Giolla Fhaolain, son of the servant of Saint Faolan, or to an English place name meaning fallow land.
A modern name with no documented source word. In India it spread after the 2012 Bollywood film Student of the Year; in the United States it also follows Shania and other Sha- names.
A 19th and 20th century variant of Juliana, the feminine of Julian, from the Roman family name Julius. It is often read as a blend of Julia and Anne.
